titleStmt.title: A Unified Framework of Five Principles for AI in Society
titleStmt.author: Luciano Floridi
Josh Cowls

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: A Unified Framework of Five Principles for AI in Society

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: SIX PUBLISHED SETS OF AI ETHICS PRINCIPLES, forty-seven principles in all, read against each other to find out whether they converge - the object is a vocabulary, not a phenomenon
span.quote: Each set of principles meets three basic criteria: they are _recent_, published within the last three years; directly _relevant_ to AI and its impact on society as a whole (thus excluding documents specific to a particular domain, industry, or sector); and highly _reputable_, published by authoritative, multi-stakeholder organizations with at least national scope.4 Taken together, they yield 47 principles.

span.label: how to solve `principle proliferation`: whether the competing declarations say the same thing under different names, or genuinely disagree
span.quote: Unfortunately, the sheer volume of proposed principles threatens to become overwhelming and confusing, posing two potential problems.1 Either the various sets of ethical principles for AI are similar, leading to unnecessary repetition and redundancy, or, if they differ significantly, confusion and ambiguity will result instead. The worst outcome would be a ‘market for principles’ where stakeholders may be tempted to ‘shop’ for the most appealing ones ( Floridi, 2019b). How might this problem of ‘principle proliferation’ be solved?

span.label: five principles - beneficence, non-maleficence, autonomy and justice imported from bioethics, plus EXPLICABILITY, argued to be new and necessary - claimed to capture all 47
span.quote: Taken together, these five principles capture every one of the 47 principles contained in the six high-profile, expert-driven documents we analysed. Moreover, each principle is included in almost every statement of principles we analyzed

span.label: method
span.quote: Taken together, these five principles capture every one of the 47 principles contained in the six high-profile, expert-driven documents we analysed. Moreover, each principle is included in almost every statement of principles we analyzed

span.label: a field generating ethical declarations faster than it can reconcile them, with `similar terms often used to mean different things` and a risk the authors name as a `market for principles`
span.quote: Unfortunately, the sheer volume of proposed principles threatens to become overwhelming and confusing, posing two potential problems.1 Either the various sets of ethical principles for AI are similar, leading to unnecessary repetition and redundancy, or, if they differ significantly, confusion and ambiguity will result instead. The worst outcome would be a ‘market for principles’ where stakeholders may be tempted to ‘shop’ for the most appealing ones ( Floridi, 2019b). How might this problem of ‘principle proliferation’ be solved?

span.label: a comparative reading of six sets chosen by three stated criteria - recent, relevant to AI and society as a whole, and published by authoritative multi-stakeholder bodies with at least national scope - mapped onto the four bioethics principles
span.term: a comparative reading of six sets chosen by three stated criteria - recent, relevant to AI and society as a whole, and published by authoritative multi-stakeholder bodies with at least national scope - mapped onto the four bioethics principles
span.quote: For this comparative analysis, we identified six high-profile initiatives established in the interest of socially beneficial AI: 1. The Asilomar AI Principles, developed under the auspices of the Future of Life Institute

span.label: the convergence is explained by a structural resemblance between the fields, and the explanation is offered rather than tested: `OF ALL AREAS OF APPLIED ETHICS, BIOETHICS IS THE ONE THAT MOST CLOSELY RESEMBLES DIGITAL ETHICS in dealing ecologically with new forms of agents, patients, and environments`
span.quote: This convergence can most clearly be shown by comparing the sets of principles with the four core principles commonly used in bioethics: _beneficence, non-maleficence_, _autonomy_, and _justice_ (Beauchamp & Childress, 2012). The comparison should not be surprising. Of all areas of applied ethics, bioethics is the one that most closely resembles digital ethics in dealing ecologically with new forms of agents, patients, and environments (Floridi, 2013). Yet while the four bioethical principles adapt surprisingly well to the fresh ethical challenges posed by artificial intelligence, they do not offer a perfect translation.

span.label: and the fifth principle is argued for FUNCTIONALLY - explicability is needed because the other four cannot be checked without it: you cannot tell whether AI is beneficent without understanding what it does, nor hold anyone to account without knowing why an outcome arose
span.quote: The addition of the principle of ‘explicability,’ incorporating both the epistemological sense of ‘intelligibility’ (as an answer to the question ‘how does it work?’) and in the ethical sense of ‘accountability’ (as an answer to the question ‘who is responsible for the way it works?’), is the crucial missing piece of the AI ethics jigsaw.

span.label: THE SAMPLE IS SIX DOCUMENTS AND THE PAPER SAYS WHERE THEY COME FROM: each `emerged either from initiatives with GLOBAL SCOPE, or from within WESTERN LIBERAL DEMOCRACIES`, and the framework `WOULD UNDOUBTEDLY BENEFIT FROM THE PERSPECTIVES OF REGIONS AND CULTURES PRESENTLY UN- OR UNDER-REPRESENTED`
span.quote: It is important to note that each of the six sets of ethical principles for AI that we analyzed emerged either from initiatives with global scope, or from within western liberal democracies. For the framework to be more broadly applicable, it would undoubtedly benefit from the perspectives of regions and cultures presently un- or under-represented in our sample.

span.label: the coverage claim and the distribution claim are DIFFERENT CLAIMS AND ONLY THE FIRST IS ABSOLUTE: the five principles `CAPTURE EVERY ONE OF THE 47`, but each principle appears in `ALMOST EVERY statement` - and the paper's own Table 1 shows IEEE missing autonomy and justice, and the Partnership missing autonomy
span.quote: Taken together, these five principles capture every one of the 47 principles contained in the six high-profile, expert-driven documents we analysed. Moreover, each principle is included in almost every statement of principles we analyzed

span.label: THE ADOPTION EVIDENCE INCLUDES BODIES THE AUTHORS SIT ON. AI4People and the EC High-Level Expert Group are counted as uptake, and the disclosure states that FLORIDI CHAIRED AI4PEOPLE, COWLS WAS ITS RAPPORTEUR, AND FLORIDI IS A MEMBER OF THE HLEG. Declared in full, and it is still the authors' framework being adopted by the authors' committees
span.quote: Indeed, the framework played a valuable role in the work of AI4People, Europe’s first global forum on the social impact of AI, which recently adopted it to propose 20 concrete recommendations for a ‘Good AI Society’ to the European Commission ( Floridi et al., 2018). Since then it has been largely adopted by the _Ethics Guidelines for Trustworthy AI_ published by the European Commission’s High-Level Expert Group on Artificial Intelligence (HLEGAI 2018 and 2019), which in turn has influenced the OECD’s _Recommendation of the Council on Artificial Intelligence_

span.label: the funding sits on the subject: the work was supported by an EPSRC hub AND BY FACEBOOK AND GOOGLE - two of the companies whose AI the framework is written to govern. Declared
span.quote: Floridi’s work was supported by (i) Privacy and Trust Stream - Social lead of the PETRAS Internet of Things research hub - PETRAS is funded by the UK Engineering and Physical Sciences Research Council (EPSRC), grant agreement no. EP/N023013/1; (ii) Facebook; and (iii) Google.

span.label: the paper leaves its central ambiguity open and says so twice: `IT IS NOT ENTIRELY CLEAR WHETHER IT IS THE PEOPLE DEVELOPING AI, OR THE TECHNOLOGY ITSELF, which should be encouraged not to do harm - in other words, whether it is FRANKENSTEIN OR HIS MONSTER against whose maleficence we should be guarding`
span.quote: Yet from these various warnings, it is not entirely clear whether it is the people developing AI, or the technology itself, which should be encouraged not to do harm; in other words, whether it is Frankenstein or his monster against whose maleficence we should be guarding. At the heart of this quandary is the question of autonomy.

span.label: and `justice` is left carrying more than one meaning inside the framework that is supposed to fix it: `elsewhere justice has STILL OTHER MEANINGS (especially in the sense of FAIRNESS)`. The unification does not reach inside the principles
span.quote: Elsewhere ‘justice’ has still other meanings (especially in the sense of _fairness_), variously relating to the use of AI to correct past wrongs such as eliminating unfair discrimination, promoting diversity, and preventing the rise of new threats to justice.

span.label: the six documents were selected by three declared criteria - recent, relevant to AI and society as a whole rather than to one sector, and published by authoritative multi-stakeholder bodies of at least national scope

span.label: artificial intelligence
span.quote: For the present purpose the artificial intelligence problem is taken to be that of making a machine behave in ways that would be called intelligent if a human were so behaving. (Quotation from the 2006 re-issue in McCarthy et al., 2006 [1955]). This is a _counterfactual_: _were_ a human to behave in that way, that behaviour _would_ be called intelligent. It does not mean that the machine _is_ intelligent, or even _thinking_.

span.label: thinking
span.quote: For the present purpose the artificial intelligence problem is taken to be that of making a machine behave in ways that would be called intelligent if a human were so behaving. (Quotation from the 2006 re-issue in McCarthy et al., 2006 [1955]). This is a _counterfactual_: _were_ a human to behave in that way, that behaviour _would_ be called intelligent. span.label: meta-autonomy
span.quote: This introduces a notion we might call ‘meta-autonomy,’ or a ‘decide-to-delegate’ model: humans should retain the power to decide which decisions to take: exercising the freedom to choose where necessary, and ceding it in cases where overriding reasons, such as efficacy, may outweigh the loss of control over decision-making. Any delegation should also remain overridable in principle (i.e., deciding to decide again).

span.label: `principle proliferation` - THE CONDITION THIS PAPER NAMES AND TREATS. Either the sets are similar, `leading to UNNECESSARY REPETITION AND REDUNDANCY`, or they differ, and `CONFUSION AND AMBIGUITY will result instead`. The worst case is named too: a `MARKET FOR PRINCIPLES` in which stakeholders `SHOP` for the most appealing
span.quote: Unfortunately, the sheer volume of proposed principles threatens to become overwhelming and confusing, posing two potential problems.1 Either the various sets of ethical principles for AI are similar, leading to unnecessary repetition and redundancy, or, if they differ significantly, confusion and ambiguity will result instead. The worst outcome would be a ‘market for principles’ where stakeholders may be tempted to ‘shop’ for the most appealing ones ( Floridi, 2019b). span.label: THE DIAGNOSIS, WHICH IS THIS PROJECT'S OWN THESIS IN ONE CLAUSE: `the underlying meaning of each of the principles IS CONTESTED, WITH SIMILAR TERMS OFTEN USED TO MEAN DIFFERENT THINGS`. A shared word list is not a shared vocabulary
span.quote: As we shall see, the underlying meaning of each of the principles is contested, with similar terms often used to mean different things. Nor are the four principles exhaustive.

span.label: explicability - FIVE NAMES FOR ONE PRINCIPLE, LISTED WITH THEIR SOURCES: `TRANSPARENCY` in Asilomar and EGE, `transparency` AND `ACCOUNTABILITY` in IEEE, `INTELLIGIBILITY` in AIUK, `UNDERSTANDABLE AND INTERPRETABLE` in the Partnership. The new term is coined to cover a thing four documents already had
span.quote: All of them refer to the need to understand and hold to account the decision-making processes of AI. Different terms express this principle: “transparency” in Asilomar and EGE; both “transparency” and “accountability” in IEEE; “intelligibility” in AIUK; and as “understandable and interpretable” by the Partnership.

span.label: explicability, as defined - TWO SENSES DELIBERATELY BOUND TOGETHER: the EPISTEMOLOGICAL sense of intelligibility (`how does it work?`) and the ETHICAL sense of accountability (`who is responsible for the way it works?`). One term carrying two questions on purpose
span.quote: The addition of the principle of ‘explicability,’ incorporating both the epistemological sense of ‘intelligibility’ (as an answer to the question ‘how does it work?’) and in the ethical sense of ‘accountability’ (as an answer to the question ‘who is responsible for the way it works?’), is the crucial missing piece of the AI ethics jigsaw.

span.label: AI - `A RESEARCH AREA IN SEARCH OF A DEFINITION` in the paper's own heading. It keeps the 1955 Dartmouth formulation, reads it as A COUNTERFACTUAL (`WERE a human to behave in that way, that behaviour WOULD be called intelligent`), and then substitutes its own working phrase - `a reservoir of smart agency on tap` - justified by fitness for the corpus it is about to analyse
span.quote: In short, AI is defined on the basis of engineered outcomes and actions and so, in what follows, we shall treat AI as a _reservoir of smart agency on tap_ (see also Floridi 2019a). This is sufficiently general to capture the many ways in which AI is discussed in the documents we analyse in the rest of this article.

span.label: beneficence and non-maleficence - `THOUGH DO ONLY GOOD AND DO NO HARM MAY SEEM LOGICALLY EQUIVALENT, THEY ARE NOT, AND REPRESENT DISTINCT PRINCIPLES`. A near-synonymy refused explicitly, which is exactly the move most papers leave implicit
span.quote: Though ‘do only good’ (beneficence) and ‘do no harm’ (non-maleficence) may seem logically equivalent, they are not, and represent distinct principles.

span.label: meta-autonomy - a coined term for `a DECIDE-TO-DELEGATE model`: humans keep the power to decide WHICH decisions to take, and any delegation must remain `OVERRIDABLE IN PRINCIPLE (i.e., deciding to decide again)`
span.quote: This introduces a notion we might call ‘meta-autonomy,’ or a ‘decide-to-delegate’ model: humans should retain the power to decide which decisions to take: exercising the freedom to choose where necessary, and ceding it in cases where overriding reasons, such as efficacy, may outweigh the loss of control over decision-making.
